# Data wrangling

## Reading in data

Which package to use?

::: {.incremental}
- `readr` for reading `.csv` files
- `readxl` for Excel files (`.xls` and `.xlsx`)
- `haven` for Stata, SPSS, and SAS files
- `googlesheets4` for reading directly from Google Sheets

:::

::: {.callout-tip}
See the reading data cheatsheet: <https://github.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/blob/main/data-import.pdf>
:::

## Reading in data

If the data are clean, it's not complicated

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
messy_data <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")
```
:::
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# Function arguments
read_csv(
  file,
  col_names = TRUE,
  col_types = NULL,
  col_select = NULL,
  id = NULL,
  locale = default_locale(),
  na = c("", "NA"),
  quoted_na = deprecated(),
  quote = "\"",
  comment = "",
  trim_ws = TRUE,
  skip = 0,
  n_max = Inf,
  guess_max = min(1000, n_max),
  name_repair = "unique",
  num_threads = readr_threads(),
  progress = show_progress(),
  show_col_types = should_show_types(),
  skip_empty_rows = TRUE,
  lazy = should_read_lazy()
)
```
:::
::::

## Renaming

`janitor::clean_names()` is a starting point

`dplyr::rename()` and `dplyr::rename_with()` let you specify names

::::: {.panel-tabset}

### Current names

```{r}
names(messy_data)
```

### `clean_names`

```{r}
messy_data |> 
  clean_names() |> 
  names()
```

### `rename`

```{r}
messy_data |> 
  rename(
    age = `Age (single year)`
  ) |> 
  names()
```

### `rename_with`

```{r}
messy_data |> 
  rename_with(
    \(x)
    paste0("y", x),
    `2011`:`2031`
  ) |> 
  names()

```

### Example

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
messy_data <- messy_data |> 
  clean_names() |> 
  rename(
    age = age_single_year
  )
names(messy_data)
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}

:::
::::
:::::

## Selecting

Keep or remove columns using `select()`

::::: {.panel-tabset}
### Keep

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
messy_data |> 
  select(age, x2011) |> 
  names()
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
Separate names using commas `,`
:::
::::

### Drop

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
messy_data |> 
  select(-age) |> 
  names()
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
Use a minus `-` to drop a variable
:::
::::

### Ranges

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
messy_data |> 
  select(age, x2011:x2016) |> 
  names()
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
Use a colon `:` connecting two variables to select them and everything in between
:::
::::

### Selectors

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
messy_data |> 
  select(
    contains("202"),
    starts_with("x"),
    where(is.numeric)
  ) |> 
  names()
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- `contains` matches against a pattern
- `starts_with` only looks at the start
- `where` keeps columns that meet a criteria
- See the `tidyselect` package
:::
::::

### Example

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
messy_data <- messy_data |> 
  select(
    age,
    contains("202")
  )

messy_data
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- We've kept the `age` variable and counts for the 2020s
:::
::::
:::::

## Filtering

Keep or remove rows using `dplyr::filter()`

::::: {.panel-tabset}

### One

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
messy_data |> 
  filter(age == "18") |> 
  nrow()
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- `age` is a character
- `==` is how to specify an equality

:::
::::
### Two

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
messy_data |> 
  filter(
    age == "18",
    x2020 > 1000
    ) |> 
  nrow()

messy_data |> 
  filter(
    age == "18" &
      x2020 > 1000
    ) |> 
  nrow()
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- `x2011` is a number
- Separating conditions with a comma is the same as using `&`

:::
::::
### OR

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
messy_data |> 
  filter(
    age == "18" |
      age == "19"
    ) |> 
  nrow()
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- The vertical bar `|` is how to specify OR
- If either condition is true, the row is kept

:::
::::
### `%in%`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
messy_data |> 
  filter(
    age %in% c("18","19","20")
    ) |> 
  nrow()
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}

:::
::::
### Example

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
messy_data <- messy_data |> 
  filter(
    between(as.numeric(age), 18, 40) | 
      age %in% c("Males", "Females")
    ) 

messy_data
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- We've kept only ages 18 to 40, or where age is `Males` or `Females`
:::
::::
:::::

## Modifying

Update an existing column or make a new one using `mutate()`

::::: {.panel-tabset}

### One variable

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| output: false
messy_data |> 
  mutate(
    var_1 = "1"
  )
```
:::
::: {.column}
- Single equals `=` to specify what the variable (`var_1`) should be

:::
::::

### Multiple variables

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| output: false
messy_data |> 
  mutate(
    var_1 = "1",
    var_2 = 2,
    var_3 = as.numeric(var_1) + var_2
  )
```
:::
::: {.column}
- Separate variables using commas
- Creating a variable on an earlier line means you can refer to it within the same `mutate()`
:::
::::

### `if_else`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| output: false
messy_data |> 
  mutate(
    var_1 = if_else(
      condition = age %in% c("18", "19", "20"),
      true = 1,
      false = 0,
      missing = 0
    )
  )
```
:::
::: {.column}
- `missing` specifies what to do if the value is `NA`
:::
::::

### `case_when`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| output: false
messy_data |> 
  mutate(
    age = as.numeric(age),
    var_1 = case_when(
      age %in% c(18, 19, 20) ~ "18 to 20",
      between(age, 21, 30) ~ "21 to 30",
      between(age, 30, 40) ~ "30 to 40",
      .default = "Other"
    )
  )
```
:::
::: {.column}
- the condition (left-side) must evaluate to TRUE or FALSE
- the value to assign if this condition is true (right-side)
- separated by a tilde `~`
- the `.default` is `NA` if you don't specify anything
- applies conditions from top to bottom
:::
::::

### Example

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
messy_data <- messy_data |> 
  mutate(
    sex = case_when(
      age == "Males" ~ age,
      age == "Females" ~ age,
      .default = NA
    ),
    age = as.numeric(age),
    age_group = case_when(
      between(age, 18, 24) ~ "18 to 24",
      between(age, 25, 40) ~ "25 to 40"
    )
  )
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- `sex` is extracted from the `age` variable
- `age` is numeric now
- `age_group` is based on age ranges
:::
::::

:::::

## Filling in missing data

`dplyr::fill()` fills in missing data using the last non-missing values

::::: {.panel-tabset}

### Before

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
messy_data$sex
```
:::
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# Function arguments
fill(
  messy_data, 
  ..., 
  .by = NULL, 
  .direction = c("down", "up", "downup", "updown")
)
```

:::
::::
### After

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
messy_data <- messy_data |> 
  fill(sex, .direction = "down")

messy_data$sex
```
:::
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# Function arguments
fill(
  messy_data, 
  ..., 
  .by = NULL, 
  .direction = c("down", "up", "downup", "updown")
)
```

:::
::::
:::::

## Reshaping data

Use `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()` to reshape datasets

::::: {.panel-tabset}
### Longer

```{r}
#| output-location: column
messy_data <- messy_data |> 
  filter(!is.na(age)) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("x"),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "count",
  )

messy_data
```

### Wider

```{r}
#| output-location: column
messy_data <- messy_data |> 
  filter(!is.na(age)) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = count,
  )

messy_data
```

:::::

## Grouping

Use `group_by()` or the `.by = ` argument

::::: {.panel-tabset}

### `group_by()`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
messy_data |> 
  group_by(age_group) |> 
  summarise(
    n_total = sum(Males) + sum(Females)
  ) |> 
  ungroup()
```
:::
::: {.column}
- When you use `group_by()`, the output remains grouped.
- Use `ungroup()` to remove the grouping
:::
::::

### `.by = `

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
messy_data |> 
  summarise(
    n_total = sum(Males) + sum(Females),
    .by = age_group
  )
```
:::
::: {.column}
- `.by` applies the grouping just for that operation, so grouping doesn't persist
- Available for:
  - `filter()` and `filter_out()`
  - `mutate()`
  - `summarise()`
  - `slice()` functions
:::
::::
:::::

## Let's practice!

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="65%"}

Going back to the `penguins` dataset

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Drop the `flip_len` variable"
data |> 
  select(-flipper_len)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Rename `bill_len` to `bill_length` and `bill_dep` to `bill_depth`"
data |> 
  rename(
    bill_length = bill_len,
    bill_depth = bill_dep
  )
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Create a variable for the ratio of bill length to bill depth"
data |> 
  mutate(
    bill_length_depth_ratio = bill_length / bill_depth
  )
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Reshape the two `bill` variables into a longer format"
data |> 
  pivot_longer(
    contains("bill"),
    names_to = "bill_measure",
    values_to = "bill_value"
  )
```
